utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll allow you to do so, but not until after I've reminded you, Mr. Gajic, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I began to ask you some questions yesterday evening about the deployment of the 52nd Military Police Battalion in the locations that you have described in paragraph 22 of your witness statement. One further matter in that regard at this stage, if I may. Can you confirm, please, that those deployments remained from March through to September of 1998? That they continued during that period.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you please look in the white bundle behind tab 1, which is provisionally marked for identification as P1152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, do we have to replace the old index by the new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it has the MFI numbers inserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You said yesterday that although there was no mini joint command between the MUP and the 52nd Military Police Battalion in those deployment areas, there were MUP patrols in those areas. And I just wanted to look, if I could, with you, please, behind tab 1 at this document dated the 23rd of March, 1998, and signed by Colonel Delic; and in particular, at the second sentence of paragraph 1 and the first bullet point. So in the B/C/S, obviously it is on page 1, as it is in the English. The second sentence of paragraph 1 reads: "It is characteristic that the area of the village of Jablanica, the village of Kravljane, the village of Radonjic, the village of Bordanic is still under the control of the Republic of Serbia MUP. We confirm this with the following facts." And then the first one is on the 22nd of March, 1998 around 1500 hours. "Belts of 7.62 calibre bullets, several bullets that fell out of the belt and food were found in several places in the area of the village of Donji Biges in the forest towards the Radonjic Lake." Pausing there for a moment. I don't know how it appears in the B/C/S version, but "Donji Biges in the forest towards Radonjic Lake" is presumably a reference to the village of Donji Bites. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, if you read the original, then you'll see that -- of course, a "G" and a "T" are very close to each other. And upon looking at it, it sounds more -- it looks more like a "T" than --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then there is a reference to the fact that the Djakovica MUP has organised an ambush in that area on the 22nd and 23rd of March but no one showed up by the morning. Now, is that an example of the sort of MUP deployment in the area around that Lake Radoniq that you were describing to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first sentence of yours and your reference to me mentioning a mini joint command indicates that we are at cross-purposes here. I said that the MUP had organised check-points through which they exercised control over the roads and the movement of people, et cetera. Whereas, a mini joint command is quite a different matter. It's a coordinating body which is set up if the army and the MUP are involved in a joint action.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for a moment. I had prefaced my question by reminding you that you told us yesterday that there was no mini joint command in the area around the lake. So that I understand. What I'm interested in is MUP patrols operating in that area. Now, you said just a moment ago that the MUP had organised check-points over the roads.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's one of the ways in which they were active. Let me remind you that throughout 1998 and in early 1999 the MUP was the main force of the activities against terrorists. We had check-points which were one method of their work; patrols were another.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for -- well, the remaining activities, they amounted to the third method of their work. They -- that was the ambushes, that's to say. So they would lay ambushes wherever they expected the KLA to be active in order to protect the features and the buildings in the general area where an ambush was expected. But these activities were separate from that of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause please. I'm -- I'm only interrupting you -- and I don't mean to be rude at all. I'm only interrupting you because we have quite a lot of material to cover and it would help me if, as far as possible, you could keep your answers relatively brief. Just to come back on the answer you've just given us. You say, the MUP deployments involved check-points on roads, patrols, and ambushes, three different types of MUP activity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now, we can see here that in this document as an example there had obviously been a MUP patrol in the area around Donji Bites and the plan for a MUP ambush. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what follows from the text here.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I just want to understand. I mean, this is obviously in the area to the east of the main Pec-Gjakova road. I just want to understand whether those patrols and ambushes of that type of activity continued on the east of the MUP -- of the main Pec-to-Gjakova road during this period from March to September, as far as you understood the position.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem lies - and I believe that I mentioned that yesterday - in the control over the roads, because this was one of the focal activities of the KLA, to cut off any -- and all of the roads and to make it impossible to use them, because they expected in this way to block the activities of the MUP, the army, and the population in general. That was one of the strategic goals throughout the time. And the MUP --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause -- pause, if you will. Pause, if you will. Again, if I could just repeat my question. In the area to the east of the Pec-to-Gjakova road, such as Donji Bites, as we see here, were there MUP patrols and ambushes taking place and planned between March and September?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what the case was when it comes to the patrols, but as for the ambushes, I wouldn't be able to tell you. I know that there were patrols throughout the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So there were patrols going on throughout the period. Leave the ambushes aside for a moment. Patrols going on throughout the period in the area to the east of the main Pec-to-Gjakova road. That's correctly understood, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And they were going on elsewhere too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I'm only interested at the moment in this particular area. And by "this particular area," I'm referring to the area to the east of the Pec-to-Gjakova road. Can -- can I ask you this: Do you know whether ambushes were -- without asking for specific dates or details -- whether ambushes were also being planned by the MUP in that region during this period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how frequently the patrols would be carried out in order to observe the area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the frequency of the patrols. What I can tell you, based on my experience and the reports I received, is that they were conditioned by the activities of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Understood. Understood. They would be armed patrols, presumably.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. Both sides were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to another topic, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, could we find some further clarification here. It covers a period of six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this document that was just shown to you, it says - and it mentions a couple -- a few villages - is still under the control of the Republic of Serbia MUP. Now, you told us that in the six months after March - March including - that there were patrols. Now, in this document, we are talking about controlling the area and most of the questions were about patrolling the area, including frequency. Now, what I'd like to know is: When these patrols went on for those six months, were those -- was the MUP forces patrolling the area still confident that they controlled the area as well by these patrols? Because you said it was conditioned by the activity of the other party. Could you tell us whether during all those six months they felt that patrolling was in the exercise of their control or was that not the situation? Could you -- if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an ongoing problem. I said that one of the strategic tasks of the KLA was to take control of the main roads and some of the secondary roads too. Taking control of roads did not imply taking control of the asphalt road itself but also the contiguous territories on both sides of the road. And MUP had the task to prevent them from doing that. That's why I said that the frequency of these patrols depended on the activities of the KLA. Oftentimes a stretch of the road would be taken control of by the MUP and then two days later the KLA would carry out a raid, taking control of the roads again, and then this posed a great problem to the MUP because it hindered the movement of the army toward the border areas where there were border units, but it also prevented the movement of civilian traffic, especially public transportation, and so on and so forth. One of the key tasks of the MUP in general was to maintain public law and order, which implied, among other matters, that there would be free movement of vehicles, persons, and so on and so forth. And, of course, the KLA had as one of their strategic goals to prevent the movement from flowing freely, because it allowed them to spread throughout the area and carry out their other activities. I don't know whether I've been able to answer your question fully, but we can see based on the orders of commanders that movement is even prohibited. Like, for instance, the order by Colonel Lazarevic that some roads are not to be used -- were not to be used at all, because they were too risky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So in short, your answer is that patrols went on, but this does not imply necessarily that there was continuous control over the area. MUP was not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MUP was not in every respect successful in achieving their aims. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just if I may to follow on from that, you said that this process of what one might call "disputed territory" applied to the contiguous territory both sides of the main road. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, road control meant not only the control of the asphalt stretch of the road but the entire belt running along both roadsides. As far as the KLA activities were concerned, they seized control of higher ground running alongside roads, and that's how they'd have these roads under their control. Secondly, they had their armed patrols moving in the area. So they had at least two ways of going about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood. And the deployments of the MUP - and I'm interested particularly in the area to the east of the main Pec-to-Gjakova road - would involve patrols in what was effectively disputed territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that -- whichever one was considered to be a problem in view of the activities of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea how many kilometres to the east of the main road you would describe as falling within that area of disputed territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. Perhaps if I had a map. If we're talking specifically about a unit or a group of the MUP, it would certainly have had control of an area covering several kilometres. And then, of course, this did not mean that they controlled that specific stretch of territory but that they would also coordinate with their adjacent units. One of the interests for the KLA was to spread and expand the territory under their control, and, of course, the task of the MUP was to prevent exactly that. And later on we will be able to see also in terms of percentages how much of the territory the KLA was able to control.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to turn to the incident that you described in your testimony yesterday, which is referred to in paragraph 23 of your statement, which was a KLA armed attack on the 52nd Military Police Battalion on the 22nd of April. And specifically I have just one matter I want to raise with you, one collection of matters. If you could turn, please, to tab 3 in this white bundle, which is annex 18 to your witness statement and marked for identification as P1022. In the B/C/S version, you will see that there are three bullet points in the bottom half of the page, which is on the second page, which are on the second page of the English translation. And this document, which is signed by Colonel Lazarevic and dated the 22nd of April describes that attack as well as another incident and lists certain measures to be taken in response. On the first bullet point, in the English translation it refers to: "Full camouflage, fortification, loose deployment, and continuous observation." I wondered if you could explain to us, please, what "loose deployment" means.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that -- let's take a squad of soldiers, numbering between 10 and 12. In order for them not to be in one place but, rather, 3 soldiers here, then the next 3 at 10 metres, and then the next 3 at 10 metres, not grouped in one location.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for that -- the reason for that -- for the activity, yes. They were spread out.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, spread out.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for them not to constitute a concentrated target, because the probability if their work came under attack was --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood. Now, you've told us that the 52nd Military Police Battalion had a number of combat groups within it. Can you give us some idea of the size of a combat group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that yesterday I mentioned two or three places around the Radonjic Lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although, I apologise, these also depended on the actual situation and the intensity of KLA operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you -- forgive me, Mr. Gajic. You told us yesterday that the 52nd Military Police Battalion had a number of combat groups within it. And I just wanted to ask you the size, the number of men approximately in one combat group.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately the level of a platoon; meaning, between 30 and 40 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you've told us in your statement at paragraph 22 where the deployments were around -- around the lake specifically, including at the base of Radonjicka Suka. With an order -- with an order for loose deployment, that would involve, would it, spreading those men in the combat group platoon out over the territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you have an idea of how the Radonjic Lake looks like and the area surrounding it. They were deployed in a form of a horseshoe from the east, west, and south, but they also moved. But they were mainly in this area. It also depended on --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood. Understood. Over what sort of area would they move when they were moving? Over what kind of geographical area? How many kilometres away from their base post approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually they didn't move at all. Just like any other unit, they had their observation posts, forward observation posts in front of the unit deployed in a certain area. They also had combat support, observing the territory in order to avoid any surprises. But the unit itself did not move.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just forgive me. I may have misunderstood you. But just a few lines earlier on, your answer is recorded as saying: "They were deployed in the form of a horseshoe from the east, west, and south, but they also moved." I just wanted some clarification of what you meant by that remark.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant by that is they had their scouts and their observers who were in a certain way providing this link, in terms of observation and surveillance between the various groups. So there was also a physical link but also technical links between them, like radio communications and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What is the movement you were referring to? Is that the movement of -- of scouts, or what is it? What's the movement that you referred to in that answer, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, surveillance and reconnoitering units. And part of the unit is billeted there and they provided their own security on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So reconnaissance and surveillance units would move around the territory? Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just like in the other army, which sets up certain observation activities in order to avoid surprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, again, can you give us some idea as to how far away from their base unit they would be deployed in reconnaissance of that kind? Or is there no limit to it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately 1 kilometre ahead of the deployment area of the unit. Up to 1 kilometre. They didn't go too much beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Is there any -- looking back at this document and the third bullet point, which records that: "All types of provocations by the local population should be prevented. And in the case of attack on unit members and features, immediately retaliate energetically and as prescribed by the rules on combat use." First of all, "all types of provocation by the local population," do you know what that expression is intended to convey?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to armed provocations. We did mention something about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is there any military significance to the expression "immediately retaliate energetically"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a phrase. It's an order and a principled attitude of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An army responds only to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, that's -- that's understood. Could we look very briefly just behind tab 4, please, in this connection. And tab 4 is marked as P1156. Could I ask you, please, on the B/C/S version to turn to page 2 and to the first three lines, which in the English translation are the last three lines on page 2, which refer back to this incident on the 22nd of April. I wonder if you could help us, because there's some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, it's MFI'd as P1157. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have it MFI'd as P1156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Behind tab 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pristina Corps -- well, that's the new -- I have to look at the new version. Yes. In your earlier -- in your earlier annex -- in your earlier index, it had a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that -- yes, that's also true for number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand the new one is the correct one and that would then be P1156.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If ever someone else at a later stage would have to consult this, then P numbers would do better. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just wonder if you can help us with the first two lines on the top of page 2, which in the English translation are the last three lines on the bottom of page 2. Without going through the detail of all of it, is there a suggestion there that a platoon should be assigned? Can you just tell us what that -- what that entry is indicating?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to, based on the consequences of the attack on men and the equipment -- are you referring to this section and the 52nd Military Police Battalion at 11.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in -- at 11.00 --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Activities -- this is not very clearly written, but as far as I can understand, this is again the case of an attack on the 52nd Military Police Battalion and it was estimated that the forces involved were approximately of a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I understand it. And the goal was to take control of this area where this part of the 52nd Battalion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much for that. Can we look, please, at tab 5, please. I'm going to take the these documents at a reasonable pace, if I may, because there are only particular passages I want to ask you about. Could we look at tab 5, please, which is P1159. And in the B/C/S version, if you could please find the number "2" about halfway down the page and then drop down seven lines to a line beginning "U toku," which in the English translation is on page 2, six lines up from the bottom and reads: "In the course of the 26th of April, 1998, the composition of the 53rd Gb entered into the composition of the 52nd IDC, Reconnaissance and Sabotage Company, which up to now was in the composition of the 52nd bVP, Military Police Battalion." Could you just explain to us, please, what that deployment indicates.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order. The 53rd Gb, which stands for the "Border Battalion" incorporates the 52nd Reconnaissance Sabotage Company, which up to then had been part of the 52nd Military Police Battalion. Mr. Emmerson, we mentioned something about that yesterday when you asked me about the scouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So here have an order for this reconnaissance unit from the 52nd Battalion be attached to the 53rd Border Battalion, in view of the problems prevailing on the border. And the duty of the scouts was precisely that, to collect intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And if you could just look, please, at item number 5 on page 2, which lists the ammunition spent by the 52nd Military Police Battalion during the past days. It doesn't say how many days. We can see that there are 7 -- I'm sorry, 6.300 7.6-millimetre bullets, for example, listed there. That would be ammunition expended by the Military Police Battalion located in the area of Lake Radoniq, would it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Can we look, please, now behind tab 7 -- I'm sorry, behind tab -- yes, behind tab 7, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before Mr. Emmerson goes on, it's just been brought to my attention. If we could just -- this may impact on documents in cross-examination. The first document Mr. Emmerson took the witness to, at page 2 of the translation under tab 1, which is P1152, and he read a -- a passage from the document saying: "It is characteristic that the area of the village of Jablanica," et cetera, "is still under the control of the Republic of Serbia MUP. We confirm this with the following facts." I've just received some advice from a translator - and this is only an unrevised translation - that the words "still under the control" should actually read "outside the control of." Which is entirely different to what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I'm having a languages -- sorry, translator revise the entire document as we speak. But I mean that could quite easily be confirmed what it actually says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course the witness has explained, since I put a specific question --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely so. That -- essentially he characterises this as disputed territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With patrolling, not necessarily controlling.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly so. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's good to have the right translation there so --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question. Could you tell me, Mr. Gajic: You said the 6.300 pieces of 7.62-millimetre bullets, you say they were fired in the Lake Radonjic area. Where do I read in this document, or is it your own memory that it was specifically there? Because this document, as far as I understand, and also the PrK units cover a wider territory than just Lake Radonjic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I may be able to assist to this extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If one looks at the immediately preceding words, it refers to ammunition expended by the 52nd Military Police Battalion. And the testimony of the witness yesterday was that the only location in Western Kosovo where the Military Police Battalion was deployed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- were the locations he describes in paragraph 22. That was the premise for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that -- was that on the basis of which you said that these 6.300 were fired there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Tabs 7, then, Exhibit P1162. Again, just a matter of interpretation, if you could, please. In the B/C/S version on page 2, under paragraph 3, five lines up from the bottom is a line beginning "1 hab 155-millimetre." Which appears on page 2 of the English translation, again under paragraph 3, of course, about halfway down the page. This is an order by Colonel Lazarevic for the 2nd of May ordering as follows: "Replenish the first 155-millimetre hab from the 2nd Battalion of the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade within the composition of the 52nd Military Police Battalion in the Lake -- I'm sorry, the Radonjic Lake sector to full MF peacetime establishment capacity (with two additional artillery pieces)." What I'm interested in at this stage, please, is for you to explain to us the relationship that is there described between the 2nd Battalion of the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade and the 52nd Military Police Brigade, because it appears that there is some transfer either of men or of equipment taking place or being ordered here. Could you just explain to us what that means.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the 1st Howitzer Battery, 150-millimetre Howitzers from the 2nd Battalion of the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade. This battery was attached in order to reinforce the 52nd Military Police Battalion, and it was ordered here to put it at full combat readiness in order for it to be able to carry out its orders by attaching it to the 52nd Military Police Battalion. So, in other words, the 52nd Military Police Battalion was reinforced in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So, again, just to make sure I've understood, does this involve the reinforcement of the forces, the 52nd Military Police Battalion forces deployed at the lake through the addition of a Howitzer battery from the 2nd Battalion of the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 52nd Battalion of the Mixed Artillery Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 8, please. In the B/C/S, fourth line down. In the English, fifth line up from the bottom. It's a single page document in the original; two pages in the English translation. I'm looking at the bottom of page 1 in the English translation. Tab 8 is marked for identification as P1038. The entry reads: "128-millimetre self-propelled multiple rocket launcher battery Oganj from the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade is to be redeployed to the sector of Radonjic Lake dam and tasked with giving infantry support to the corps units pursuant to a special order." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that a -- is that a further and separate reinforcement of the forces of the 52nd Military Police Battalion or is it the same one as we were just looking at?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This has nothing to do with the 52nd Battalion. In the area of the Radonjic Lake dam, I think that this Military Police Battalion was not there. But this is generally this area, the general area that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Where do you understand -- I'm sorry. Where do you understand the Radonjic Lake dam to be? Just approximately. If you can describe it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a canal called Bistrica, but I cannot tell you exactly without a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, help me. If I can -- we know that there is a canal that runs into the lake. And we know that there are loch gates in one end of the canal at Lluka e Eperme. Is that what you're referring to as the dam?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the part. But, Mr. Emmerson, what I wanted to say here was that this unit here, Oganj, was part of the 52nd Military -- had it been part of the 52nd Military Police Battalion, it would have been referred to in the same way as it was referred earlier to the Howitzer Battery. In other words, they are totally unrelated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood. But just so that we -- so that we can try to understand what this entry means, this is a deployment of the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade to the area of Lluka e Eperme at the other end of the canal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, one could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's tasked with giving infantry support to corps units pursuant to a special order. Now, what -- infantry support pursuant to a special order. Can you help us with that, please, as to what we are to make of that, how we are to interpret that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a kind of preventative order or pre-emptive order based on the actual situation prevailing on the ground and the estimate of the possible further development. The command decided to undertake certain pre-emptive measure by engaging this formation with the rocket launcher system Oganj. This does not mean that this system was actually engaged. An army always takes some preventative measures in order to avoid surprises. So this was dictated by an actual intelligence and security and tactical situation to launch this kind of pre-emptive move.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood. Understood. We don't know, obviously, from this document whether that battery was ever used.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But we do -- but we do know it was deployed. Is that correct? To that area. Yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You can see it from this document. But what I'm trying to explain to you is that there were certain conditions and parameters so that you can get a general idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood. I'm only interested at this stage in deployments. Infantry support -- now, to a layperson, "infantry support" suggests ground troops. Is that what we're to understand by this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only infantry measures -- well, yes, generally infantry, because infantry is -- or was mostly involved in this combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Understood. All I'm trying to do is to make sure we've understood this particular entry in the document. So, again, from the answers you've given, may I see if I've understood correctly. This is an order deploying a 128-millimetre self-propelled multiple rocket launcher battery and infantry support to the area you've described.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that -- please. But given the range, it could have been some other area or artillery. But as you also underlined, this was under a special order. It could not have been used unless it was estimated that there was the need for using it, because it's a very powerful system.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know what level of infantry support would come with the Oganj system? Would accompany it? Some indication.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oganj was most commonly used before an action was launched. That's the so-called artillery -- artillery preparation before an action is carried out. A certain territory, so to speak, covered with fire from Oganj in order to isolate it, and after that the infantry moves in. So that was its purpose. Basically that was its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Not long-range fire from the fire system, followed by infantry support moving through the territory is what we would expect.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I -- just for -- for further certainty, I'd like to again spend a few words on the Lake Radonjic dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, our understanding of the Lake Radonjic water household is that there is a river. From this river, there is a dam in this river, Lluka e Eperme. There is an inlet to the canal which takes you quite a lot of kilometres down. For you it would be south-easterly direction. Then the water from this canal flows into the lake. And then at the end of the lake, there is a dam which keeps the water at a certain level so that electricity, I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the filtration system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And a filtration system. Now, Mr. Emmerson went with you through the words "the sector of the Radonjic Lake dam." And I think you identified that it would be the inlet system and not the end of the lake. Is that correctly understood that the reference to "the Radonjic Lake dam" is not the dam at the very end of the lake where the water then further flows down? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said when I mentioned the inlet part, I mentioned Bistrica. This section is called Bistrica, and it enters the canal. And the other thing referred to the outlet, Lluka and things -- other issues that you mentioned. And it was explained how this system functioned. And I had an opportunity myself to see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sector of Radonjic Lake dam is the beginning and not the end of the system. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Tab 10, if I may, please. This is marked as P833, which means presumably that we've seen it -- yes, of course we have, seen it elsewhere. P833, which is annex 16 to your witness statement. And I asked you yesterday about army special units or KSJ. I wonder if you could help me, please, with this. It's a little difficult because of the numbering on these pages, but if you look in the B/C/S version, on the bottom right-hand corner you will find that the alternate pages are numbered as 2 and 4. And I'm looking for the page in the B/C/S with the number "4" at the bottom right and the number "5" typed at the top. And so far as the English translation is concerned, the passage that I'm looking at appears on page 6 at point 2. First of all, Mr. Gajic, just to -- just to repeat that, you're looking in the B/C/S version at the page which has "5" typed at the top, the number "5" at the top, and a number "4" written in handwriting at the bottom. Do you have that page? If you just take it through from the beginning to page 5. And we need to come down the page on the screen, because the -- the point I want to ask you about is paragraph 2.2 on that page, little 2. So paragraph 2.2 little 2. The translation reads: "Propose" -- this is -- I'm sorry, just place this in its proper context, this is a submission by Major-General Pavkovic to the Pristina Corps Command of the 13th of May, assessments and recommendations. And at 2.2, little 2 on the relevant page, the entry reads: "Propose to the VJ GS the engagement of KSJ, or special corps -- special units corps, units to replace the 52nd bVP, BG-2 of the 549th Motorised Brigade and BG-2 of the 125th Motorised Brigade for rest and replenishment and in order to carry out anti-terrorist operations." Now, first of all, this appears, would you agree, to be a proposal made by Major-General Pavkovic to the General Staff? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me have a look at this. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a proposal for the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he proposes the engagement of KSJ units to replace the 52nd Military Police Battalion, first of all. So that would presumably involve putting the KSJ units in the area that you've described as the deployment positions around Lake Radoniq; is that correct? That's what he's proposing.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To replace the 52nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that happen, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it did. And the reasons for it are stated here. For rest. They had to rotate units, which was a common thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I -- I'm just asking, because I asked you yesterday whether there were KSJ units deployed in the areas that you described in paragraph 22 of your statement, and I thought you told us yesterday that there were not. But in fact does this now refresh your memory that there were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the question had to do with the 52nd Military Police Battalion yesterday but, rather, the engagement of the KSJ. And I answered in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There may have been a misunderstanding. But anyway, the position is that special -- special units were deployed to the areas you describe in paragraph 2, around Lake Radoniq and the foot of Suka Radoniq sometime after the 13th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Along with the two combat groups mentioned herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, just help us with this. Just to understand what this paragraph is saying. Is it saying that the special units corps should be redeployed to replace the Military Police Battalion together with BG-2 of the 549th and 125th? In other words, that the special units and BG-2 of the 549th and BG-2 of the 125th should then be deployed to the Lake Radoniq area? Is that how we're to understand it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's stated here in quite precise terms, and I'll read this: "Propose to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army to the engagement of special units corps for -- to replace the 22nd Military Police Battalion and the Combat Group 2 of 549th Motorised Brigade and the BG-2 of 125th Motorised Brigade," which means that the KSJ units were to replace all these units: The 52nd Military Police Battalion and the two combat groups, and they were to be replaced by KSJ units.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was the alternative interpretation. I wasn't sure which was correct. And it ends by saying: "For rest and replenishment and in order to carry out anti-terrorist operations." So can I understand how in the B/C/S version that is to be interpreted. Who is to be carrying out the anti-terrorist operations? The troops that are doing the replacement - that is to say, the KSJ - or the troops who are being temporarily relieved?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the superior command decided to launch an anti-terrorist operation - and we know that it started in late July - then the KSJ would be engaged in those activities, and that's to say, the unit replacing the three other formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: See, we know that there was a -- a -- there were a series of operations in which there were -- let me put it neutrally -- significant engagements at the end of May in the area along the main Peje-to-Gjakova road and villages around. We can see here that there is a proposal to free up troops and make them available for anti-terrorist operations. And we have already had some testimony from Colonel Zivanovic of the 125th that authorisation for the VJ to engage in anti-terrorist operations was not given until the second half of June. Now, can -- can you help us, please. Were the VJ permitted under authority of the General Staff to engage in anti-terrorist operations before the second half of June?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite precise about this. I don't know what General Zivanovic said. But only on the 28th of July, 1998 was a directive adopted to carry out the anti-terrorist operation, which was in fact carried out under the code name "Grom-3."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: End of July through to September, when it was supposed to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And -- and that was the operation that began with a sweep from Peje along the main road towards Kijevo and up towards Malisevo in Central Kosovo; is that right? With Malisevo falling to Serb forces at the end of July.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that the sweeping of the terrain was the main objective. The objective was to basically carry out a crackdown on all the terrorist forces in -- not only in the Dukagjin Operational Zone. These forces had grown to such an extent that the army was unable to do anything else but to launch an offensive. Up to that point, up to that anti-terrorist operation, there were clashes with the KLA, but they only grew in intensity, starting in the month of April and May. And then in time -- or rather, there came a time when this operation had to be launched. And what it says here --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you? It's my fault. I asked you for confirmation of which offensive you were referring to, and I'm going to come back to ask you some questions about the end of July offensive and what occurred during it in -- in a little while, if I may. I just wanted to make sure we understood one another as far as authorisation was concerned. Still in this document, please, behind tab 10. If you could look, please, to the front page and to the fourth and fifth paragraphs under the -- the figure "1" which again, of course, are on page 1 of the English translation. This is a document dated the 13th of May of 1998 and gives, as we can see in the fourth paragraph, an estimate of 3 and a half to 4.000 members of the KLA armed and trained for armed raids and guerilla operations and goes on to suggest that the terrorist forces are increasingly taking on the attributes of a military organisation and setting up units from platoon to company size. Now, I think in your evidence yesterday in answer to a question from Mr. Re you suggested that during the first three months of 1998 -- forgive me for a moment. Between January and March it was counter-intelligence's estimation that there were up to 3.000 armed men who had organised themselves. I just want, if I may, to give you an opportunity to comment on the assessment of this document by the British military attache to Belgrade, who was invited to assess these estimates and this particular document during testimony he gave in the Limaj trial, which is behind tab 10A in the bundle. And I'm particularly interested in pages 1919 to 1920. I'm just going to read you a very short extract of Colonel Crosland's testimony in another trial concerning the estimate as it appears in this very document. He says: "I think the numbers that General Pavkovic replies to is a very debatable area. I myself had said that I thought there were between 400 and 500 what I would call hard-core KLA. It is difficult to say who is correct. If he is taking into account the potential numbers that were apparently and possibly training in Albania itself, then those numbers are 3 and a half thousand to 4 and a half thousand, not too far-fetched." Can I understand the position. When you gave the evidence that you gave yesterday and the figures that you gave, were you taking account of potential recruits from outside of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yesterday I said that up until the month of March there were roughly 3.000 members of the KLA who were both armed and organised. I also said that in our estimates there were between 6 and 8 thousand of those who wielded weapons. So there's a big difference between the numbers of those organised in some formations and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You also --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is a realistic figure. I did not, in other words, take into consideration members of the KLA who were undergoing training in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's also a vast difference, as I'm sure you'll agree, between Colonel Crosland's estimate of 4 to 5 hundred active organised members and yours; a difference of tenfold.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make two points here. I hold the Colonel Crosland in high esteem. I know him personally. I know him to be a true professional. Based on what you read, he said that there were between 400 and 500 extremist members of the KLA. So he spoke of the nucleus. He did not speak of their numbers in general. He only mentioned the most extremist ones. With all due respect to Colonel Crosland, we were much more familiar with the situation in the field. He had been in the service in Yugoslavia for three years, and we had been dealing with the matters in Kosovo for over ten years and we were more aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony yesterday that the assessments that you received from the RDB were not always accurate. I just want to come back to this transcript, if I may, because Colonel Crosland goes on to comment on Major-General Pavkovic's assessment in this document of organisation into battalions. And this is at line 17 on 1919. Having been asked about this comment about setting up the KLA, setting up platoons and companies in May, the 13th of May, as --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only have this in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I understand that. And I'm going to read it to you so that it can be translated to you into B/C/S. He says: "I think, with respect to Your Honours, it is very difficult to look at a terrorist organisation in the same light as regular forces who are based on specific organisation of platoon, i.e., 30 persons to a company -- to a company of 100 to a battalion or a regiment of between 400 and 600 men. I personally visited about five or six KLA headquarter bases scattered throughout Kosovo during my time there. And I would say at this stage in May they were not as organised as General Pavkovic is saying. I mean, he may have been using this for his own propaganda, and any general facing an insurgency as this was is bound to put a more glossy view on the opposition in order to ensure that he gets the correct support to deal with the problem that was a very real problem and a growing problem. But to say it was as organised within platoon and company, you know, 30- and 100-man units, I think it was possibly stretching the credibility at this particular time. There was a basic area of command control, but I stress basic, and that was basically against mainly linear - either a road or a river - into which area a headman would have what I would describe token authority." So Colonel Crosland is here accusing, in the nicest possible way, Major-General Pavkovic of exactly what you're accusing the RDB of, as I understand it, which is exaggerating the figures for propaganda reasons in order to secure the resources that are required. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not fully agree with Colonel Crosland. That's his view of the matter, which was slightly partial, and one knows why. What was characteristic was that until the month of March the KLA had predominantly been organised in groups. That's true. We're talking about the end of 1997 through to the month of March 1998, and these groups numbered three, five, ten men, up to the maximum of thirty. They were attached to certain staffs that had been established in villages. These were village staffs. They had a body coordinating this, which was called either the Main Staff or a staff of sorts. And they were not that closely connected. After that, they embarked on setting up a military formation starting from the month of April, May, and especially June, because we know that brigades were set up in June. On the 21st of June, Krasniqi - you have that footage, I believe - set up a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause for a moment. Let us catch up with you. I think maybe you're referring to July, are you, for the establishment of the Adrijan Krasniqi Brigade, rather than June? I mean, it's quite important that we get dates right, Mr. Gajic. It's quite important that we understand the accuracy of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of June, 1998 in Tirana, Ahmet Krasniqi, who you know was killed later on, and so on and so forth, gave -- handed wartime flags to the commander of 134th Brigade. Zemaj was the commander. Two more brigades were set up, 131st and 133rd Brigade. 134th Brigade, together with their men, crossed over to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I understand now the testimony --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late June.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand now what it is you're referring to. In June. Finally this, just before we -- I suggest a break. Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the Chamber would like to deliver a few decisions as well. So if within two or three minutes you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just finally, could you look in your annexes -- I'm afraid it's not in the white bundle -- to tab 4, which is P1442. If it could be brought up on the screen, please. And I'm interested, if I may, in the B/C/S in the third paragraph on page 1; and in the English, in the first paragraph on page 2. This is a document dated the 23rd of February, issued by Colonel Delic, assessing the strength and composition at the end of February -- or the 23rd of February, I'm sorry, of KLA deployment and forces in his area of responsibility, which he describes in the first paragraph as covering the territory of Djakovica both in the border area villages of Junik, Batusa, Morina, Ponosevac, Seremet, and in the Djakovica town, specifically in the eastern side of the Beli Drim River and the Decanska Bistrica river to the north until the village of Vrhovac to the west, Lake Radonjic, and to the south, the Crmljane bend, an area he describes as 90 square kilometres, including, as far east as Jablanica. In the third paragraph, his assessment, which is based upon a reliable MUP source, is as follows: "A reliable source MUP told us that up to 200 members of the so-called KLA are occasionally staying in this area, feeling totally safe. Among them are many of the Siptar terrorists wanted by MUP. In addition to the unconfirmed number of armed members of the so-called KLA, the majority of the estimated 200 men is engaged, according to the system, a peaceful farmer by day, a KLA terrorist by night." So as far as I understand it - and correct me if I'm wrong - what Colonel Delic is saying as of the 23rd of February is that in a 90-square-kilometre area stretching from the border as far east as Jablanica, the estimate regarded as reliable was a total of 200 so-called members of the KLA, the majority of whom were farmers by day, soldiers by night. Is that how you understood the position at the end of February?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have not read this properly. First of all, the period is the last months of 1997 and early January of 1998, which goes to confirm what I've been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Forgive me --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then it says the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Forgive me. This document is an assessment of the state of affairs as of the 23rd of February, is it not? You see the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But it refers to the last months of 1997 and early January. That's one thing. The other thing is that he speaks of 200 members of the KLA, armed, and so on and so forth --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who are under arms at all times and a greater number of them are engaged, and so on and so forth. So there are 200 of them who are organised, and most of the 200 are farmers by day and then soldiers by night.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood the paragraph to mean. So a total of 200 --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then my apologies are in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: A total of --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organised. Plus those who are farmers by day and carrying out actions by night. So it would -- the number would be far greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, a total of -- is -- a total of 200 who are organised; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to this, in late 1997 and early January of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And does it --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was written in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Does it go on to say: "A majority of the estimated 200 men is engaged according to a peaceful farmer by day, KLA soldier by night" system?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a characteristic of them in general. They'd change into civilian clothes and then you'd have the person farming the land and then at night changing into a uniform, taking up arms, and carrying out actions. That was the tactics that they used. And they were successful in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not entirely clear to me whether you say those farmers by day, KLA soldiers by night, are these in addition to the 200 organised people, or are they part of these 200 organised people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Above the number of 200. So there's more than the ones who were organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And again, that description, you would say, was correct, would you? The description that appears here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because this was an assessment of the situation as at the end of 1997 and the beginning of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Gajic, we'll have a break for -- for you it will be approximately half an hour. The Chamber would like to deliver -- to deliver some decisions, but I ask already Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom so that you can enjoy your coffee rather than listen to decisions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I'm here to be called upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the first which I will read is not actually a decision but, rather, an inquiry. It is an inquiry into whether the Defence has any further submissions relating to the notes of Witness 29. The Chamber would like to address the matter relating to Witness 29's notes. The parties will recall that the issue was left at the stage where on the 26th of April, 2007, after the witness had finished testifying, the Chamber ordered that on his return home, the witness should hand over to VWS any remaining notes referred to in his witness statement that he still had in his possession. On the 30th of May, 2007, a legal officer from the Chamber handed these notes to the Prosecution with the instruction that copies should be made available to the Defence. Since this time, the Chamber has heard nothing further on the issue from the parties. The Chamber would like therefore to ask the parties if they intend to raise any further issues on this matter. Should they choose not to do so, the Chamber will consider the matter to be closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate straight away that unless anybody corrects me, the direction that the Trial Chamber gave has not been carried into effect. Those notes have not been provided to Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's ... Then I think the instruction was that the notes handed to the Prosecution were given with the instruction that copies should be made available to the Defence. Has this happened, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I absolutely have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please try to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am taken entirely by surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not blame anyone for not having these details immediately available, but would you please inquire into the matter. Then the Chamber would like to deliver a decision on the admission of the Visnjic report and his resume. On the 12th of September, 2007, the Chamber heard the evidence of Mr. Visnjic, who testified about ballistics and an examination of bullet casings he conducted in 1998. The Prosecution tendered through this witness document P916, which is a ballistics report made by the witness on the 2nd of December, 1998 with accompanying correspondence, and P917, which is the resume of Mr. Visnjic. The admission of this report has already been the subject of a number of filings in this case. An overview of those filings is to be found in the Chamber's written decision on the Defence motion to exclude ballistics evidence and the Prosecution application to add Mr. Visnjic as a witness, filed on the 28th of August of this year. The Defence opposes the admission of the report on the grounds that it is irrelevant, that it has no probative value, that it is not sufficiently specific, that the bullet casings that Mr. Visnjic examined are no longer available, that his personal notes have been destroyed, and that a report from another examiner, who, according to Mr. Visnjic, gave a second opinion on his conclusions, is missing as well. For more details on the parties' submissions on the issue, we again refer to our decision of the 28th of August and the references therein. According to the report and the witness's own testimony, Mr. Visnjic compared bullet casings found at Lake Radonjic with bullet casings found in the village of Gramocelj on the 24th of March, 2007, following an incident there. It is the Prosecution's case that the incident in Gramocelj in fact took place in Glodjane, in the vicinity of Mr. Haradinaj's house. Therefore, the subject matter of the report is relevant to an issue in this case and, as a result, the document meets the relevance test for the admission of evidence. We note that the arguments raised by the Defence in opposition to the admission of the report go to the weight of his -- this evidence and will be considered by the Chamber in due course. Without any prejudice to future considerations of the evidence given by Mr. Visnjic, the Chamber holds the view that the report is the indispensable basis of Mr. Visnjic's testimony which has served the Chamber to better understand the background in which the report was made. It would make no sense at this stage to have Mr. Visnjic's testimony in evidence but not the report around which that testimony revolves. What weight, if any, will finally be given to Mr. Visnjic's conclusions is a different matter that needs not to be decided at the admissibility stage. Therefore, the report is admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 89(C) of the Rules. As to P917, the resume of Mr. Visnjic, the Chamber considers it relevant as it provides information about Mr. Visnjic's education and experience in the field of ballistics, and in light of the aforementioned, we also admit that document into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. The last decision the Chamber delivers is a decision not to recall Professor Lecomte. The Chamber will address the issue of whether Professor Lecomte should be recalled. On the 3rd of October, 2007, Professor Lecomte testified in this case as a witness for the Prosecution. At the end of the court day, and approximately one hour into re-examination, the Prosecution indicated that they still had some questions that they wanted to put to the witness. It was not possible to ask the witness to return the following day, as she had to return to her home country for a court appearance. The Defence, on being asked if they would join in requesting that the witness to be recalled to enable them to put further questions to her took no position on the matter. The Chamber then informed the parties that it would consider whether to grant the Prosecution's request. The Chamber has carefully reviewed the transcript of Professor Lecomte's evidence and is of the view that the matters for which she was called to give evidence have been sufficiently covered. The Chamber therefore decides that there is no need to recall the witness. In reaching this decision, the Chamber has also noted that the Defence does not insist on putting any further questions to the witness after the completion of her re-examination. The Chamber invites the Victims and Witness Section to inform the witness that she will not be required to return to complete her re-examination in this case. And this concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. We will have a break until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr.. Gajic, could you turn to tab 13, please, in the white bundle, which is Exhibit D75. This is a document not annexed to your witness statement but is a 23rd of June order of Colonel Lazarevic for the formation of Combat Group 5 with, as in paragraph 1 indicates, various constituent elements. And in paragraph 2, the deployment of Combat Group 5 to the Donji Bites village sector by Radonjicka Suka by 1500 hours on the 23rd of June. Do you see that? Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then a task is set out which is that BG-5 in coordinated action with the 52nd Military Police Battalion and making use of Radonjicka Suka should prevent operations by the DTS along a series of axes and the axes are there set out. The first is Rznic to Glodjane to Donji Bites. The second is Gornji Ratis to Donji Ratis to Rakoc. And the third is Gramocelj to Donji Bites. Now, obviously we know the geography of that area and the various points on those three axes. I just wanted you to help us, if you could, please. How would a joint action between a combat group -- a newly established combat group and the 52nd Military Police Battalion, how would they set about preventing KLA activities along, for example, an access -- an axis stretching from Donji Bites up to Rznic? What would they do in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is a pre-emptive order, because based on the situation, surveillance thereof, DTS activities were -- DTS stands for sabotage and terrorist forces along this axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, the army was preparing itself for such an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This coordinated action, however, would be in response to such an attack. The Military Police Battalion will use its combat resources to respond to the attack, and the BG would also respond with what they had at their disposal by engaging these DTS forces attacking these two units. In other words, the army would not have acted before an actual attack took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood. But --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So they would just act in response. This is a response to an expected or anticipated attack or attacks, because we are talking here about three axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that. How does the joint force, this joint BG-5 and 52nd Military Police Battalion force, how do they, for example, secure the area of Rznic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In order to prevent -- in order to be in a position to prevent KLA operations starting in Rznic, what exactly do they do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was an action along this axis, they would use their firing systems to engage these forces. So if you have an armed group coming your way and its goal is to attack a certain group of the 52nd Military Police Battalion, the battalion would respond in order to prevent the attack, incur losses, take captives, et cetera. Therefore, in anticipation of an attack, measures need to be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you turn, please, behind tab 14 now. And this is Exhibit D179, which is a letter of the 23rd of July from Colonel General Perisic to the President of the Republic, Mr. Milosevic. And I just wanted to ask your help, please, to see if you could assist with one matter, given the seniority of your position at the time. Could you turn to paragraph 3, subparagraph (a) of this letter. So paragraph 3 is on page 4 of the English translation and on the third page of the B/C/S original. It reads: "Constant aspirations by members of the MUP to have some VJ units subordinated to them leads to misunderstandings if the units are not given, and if they are given, this represents unauthorised and unprofessional use, which has counter-effects, the best examples being Decani and Orahovac." Now, obviously -- so this is General Colonel Perisic writing to Mr. Milosevic to raise a number of concerns on the 23rd of July. So just before the end of July operation you've described. Do you know what that is a reference to, "attempts by the MUP to have VJ units subordinated to them"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a constant problem in relation to re-subordination of units. Namely, under the law it was very clear. In the event of an emergency situation or a state of war and an escalation of a situation on the ground, the MUP may be re-subordinated. That's one of the articles on the -- of the law of the Yugoslav Army stipulates. It can be stipulated -- it can be re-subordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia and not vice versa. As you read this, it indicates that the MUP strived outside the law to re-subordinate the army to it, and this is from which misunderstandings occurred and this is what the general mentioned in his letter to President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now I just need you to explain that in a little more detail. What attempts -- what sort of attempts were the MUP making to have the VJ units subordinated to them? How did they go about it and what attempts were made and by whom? You say it was a constant problem.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was a constant problem relating to re-subordination. There was an outstanding question about the MUP being re-subordinated to the VJ under the law. However, in these specific circumstances, they requested that their commander become a superior commander to the commander of the VJ, which was contrary to the law and which the army never allowed to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But General Perisic thought that this should be drawn to some somebody's attention, because he was -- to the Commander-in-Chief's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you say it never happened. If we just look at the paragraph in detail, it seems to say: "The aspirations by the MUP to have VJ units subordinated to them leads to misunderstandings if the units are not given, and if they are given, this represents unauthorised and unprofessional use, which has counter-effects." Would you agree the suggestion appears to be that there have been some instances in which the units of the VJ have not been given and some instances in which they have, which have produced counter-effects?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it so harsh and decisively. I would interpret it rather by saying that the army perhaps allowed for a possibility in a coordinated action to grant certain commanding requests coming from the MUP contrary to what was strictly ordered. So there was a mild deviation there which then demonstrated to be dysfunctional and wrong. However, the army never allowed the MUP commanders to command the army throughout the whole period.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And do you know what the -- where it says "the best examples being Decani and Orahovac," do you know what the reference to Decani indicates there? Do you remember any specific instance of either an attempt to re-subordinate the VJ to the MUP or -- occurring in Decani?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably some MUP action involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Finally on this topic, just -- just by reference to the answers you've already given, we've heard some testimony from Colonel Crosland that on the 28th of July he came across a mixed strike force on the main Peje-to-Pristina road close to Lapusnik, poised to launch an attack on Malisevo which was commanded by Milorad Ulemek, or Milorad Lukovic, or Legija, a JSO commander who claims to be in command of a force that included VJ soldiers. Now, did that sort of event occur, Mr. Gajic? Joint forces of JSO and MUP together but with a, for example, JSO commander in overall control?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say categorically that special operation units from the State Security Service were never under the command of the VJ, nor were they ever engaged at the request or an order by the VJ.
