They were a State Security Service formation engaged along the lines of service and in cooperation with the Serbian MUP. Therefore, never. We were always absolutely against this kind of engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was not up to us. This was a legitimate and legal formation, a special unit of the State Security Service, and they were engaged according to their own plans. The army had never had any paramilitary groups within its ranks. It only had voluntary units that were organised on very strict rules and principles governing these matters. We never had any paramilitary formation or group in our ranks. And we were very -- extremely stringent on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you class the JSO or Red Berets as paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were a legal formation, a special unit, as part of the State Security Service; just as SAG was part of the MUP, the special operation units were part of the State Security Service. So in general, it was also a MUP unit, because it is probably well known that MUP had two sectors: Public security sector and state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. So -- so -- and finally on this topic, a very short answer, if I could ask for it. You would rule out, would you, the possibly that Milorad Ulemek could have been in charge of a joint strike force at the end of July which included VJ forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 15, please. This is D170. This is a letter from the following year, May 1999, from Colonel General Pavkovic to the Supreme Command Staff. And I want to ask you about paragraph 4. Paragraph 4 reads: "It has been established beyond doubt, and we have already reported on it in regular combat and other reports, that due to the non-compliance with the re-subordination orders, some MUP members and to a considerable extent entire smaller units which 'operate' independently on the ground are committing serious crimes against the Siptar civilian population in settlements or refugee centres -- shelters - murder, rape, plunder, robbery aggravated, theft, et cetera, and they then purposefully attribute or plan to attribute those crimes to units and individuals in the VJ." Now, pausing there for a moment, Mr. Gajic. Can I understand, did you see regular combat and other reports that made allegations against the MUP of that kind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period of NATO bombing of the FRY, I was at the command post with the Supreme Command Staff as the chief of security administration, so I can categorically say that not a single combat report did not contain this kind of allegations that are here under item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause, please. There's a double negative in your answer. You say, "Not a single combat report did not contain," as it's been translated. Does that mean to say every report did contain such allegations? Is that what you're trying to indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It shouldn't be a double negative. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then it's an interpretation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you say none of the reports you received contained any allegations of crimes committed by the MUP. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically say "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that covers the whole period of 1998 and 1999, does it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole period.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And so far as this letter is concerned, then, this would be the first time you'd heard such allegations being made; is that correct? The first time you'd heard that such allegations were being made at the time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw this letter when I testified in another trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in view of my position, had this document arrived at the Supreme Command Staff, I should have seen it. I must have seen it. Secondly, this is addressed to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, but letter did not receive a file number. It was just filed by the sender but was not filed with the recipient, which is inadmissible, which probably indicates that it never arrived. I don't know what happened. Actually, I do know, but it's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not entirely irrelevant. What did happen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that something was done subsequently, because the document was drafted on the 25th of May and after checking the registration, it was found out that it was registered on the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you're suggesting somebody has been tampering with the records. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't know at all. Probably General Pavkovic can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As far as the signature is concerned, everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I see. We're going to come back to this question of -- of allegations being reported in relation to the MUP in a little while, if I may. Can I turn to another topic briefly with you. You gave some evidence yesterday about annex 3 to your witness statement, which is in the white file at tab 22, just to remind you. And for the record, that is exhibit marked for identification P1141. And there's just one aspect of it I want to ask you about in a little more detail. You -- you were taken by Mr. Re to the entry which records the presence of Arkan on the territory of Zvecan municipality together with members of the Serbian Guard and his arrival in the area by helicopter. Now, this is a report dated the 23rd of January, 1998. Now, when you gave evidence about this yesterday, you said that the reason why such a matter would be included in a counter-intelligence report was because, first of all, the army considered this to be a paramilitary formation. And then you said this: "They were in contacts with the State Security Service, but in the army's view, they were a paramilitary formation. There existed a strict order of the Chief of Staff according to which paramilitary forces and groups should not be allowed access into Kosovo and Metohija. Therefore, they arrived there without the approval or the knowledge of the army and it was considered that this ought to be included in the report. Besides, there were great problems precisely with that formation. There had been great problems with that formation ever since 1991." Now, we'll just let the transcript catch up. I just want to understand the position here. You were aware of this report being made in January presumably.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And it was signed by my subordinate, Mr. Aco Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you say, then, in relation to this report that "they," that is Arkan's unit, "were in contact with the State Security Service," what was the basis for that assessment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an assessment. The fact was that they were engaged in their tasks with the MUP the whole time. They treated it as a kind of back-up formation. They didn't have a very clear view, but it was based on the rules and -- and the service as a serious institution abided by the rules. They couldn't have been treated as volunteers, because if that were the case, they should have passed the proper procedure for volunteers. So in our eyes, they were a paramilitary formation engaged by the MUP. And what you read just now, I stand by it and I'm not going to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just to be clear, you used the expression "State Security Service" yesterday, rather than public security service. You're referring to the RDB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the RDB. But it couldn't have been done without the knowledge of the public security sector in the MUP of Serbia. So as I said, there were two sectors: The public sector and the state security sector. Two sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At this point in January 1998, did you know how many men were in Arkan's formation or where they were deployed to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were never fewer than 30 of these formations, and they were mostly engaged on the axis between Pristina, due south, to Kosovo Polje, Zvecan and places like that, so in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they remained in Kosovo throughout 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They would come and go, come and go. And we mentioned this problem at the meeting with Mr. Milosevic on the 17th of May, 1999, when we said that we knew about the existence of this formation down there and that they had done certain things that were in contravention of the International Law of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we were told that sanctions were going to be imposed or taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me just take you up on that, if I may, for a moment, because I think you were tasked, were you not, by the VJ during 1999 to investigate the presence of irregular, that is, illegal paramilitary groups operating on the territory of Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we investigated this and reported, and everything was proven to be correct. And now some of the members of this paramilitary formation - one of them was already convicted, who was also in Kosovo, and a week ago four of them were arrested and are going to be prosecuted for war crimes. So there's intense work on punishing all those who committed war crimes in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the state -- states of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment. When you gave evidence in the Milutinovic case, you suggested that a number of the paramilitary formations that you discovered were operating on the territory of Kosovo would be issued with SAJ uniforms so that they would be indistinguishable from the MUP forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had either MUP or SAJ uniforms, since we knew some of them personally from the previous period, we knew who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you mentioned the meeting with President Milosevic on the 17th of May. You were present at that meeting. Was the head of the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was the head of the RDB, Radomir Markovic, present at that meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And during the course of that meeting, did Mr. Markovic raise one particular paramilitary group, known as the Skorpions, under the control of someone called Slobodan Medic, or Boka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We raised this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And help me. Is it correct that your understanding was that that group had -- had entered Kosovo having been facilitated in entering by General Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Vlastimir Djordjevic, aka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, what was the nickname?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlastimir Djordjevic, aka Rodja.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And what was his role, if any, in bringing the Skorpions into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the assistants of the Serbian interior minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was within his purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've told us that these were an illegal paramilitary grouping. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an illegal one. It was entirely legal. They didn't come covertly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Well, then perhaps you can just help me with this. Is it right that you discovered that at the end of March, the 31st of March, 1999, that group had been involved in an incident in Podujevo in which ten children and two adults had been killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it an incident. It's a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st of March, they killed 14 innocent civilians of Albanian ethnicity. Among them were women and children. One of the members of the group who participated in this, Sasa Cvijan was sentenced to 24 years of imprisonment. And as I said a moment ago, four of them were arrested a week ago since they are suspected perpetrators of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: After that crime, the Skorpions were moved off the territory of Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken back to Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did they come back into Kosovo again?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for a shorter period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's getting a long way from the indictment period. We're in March 1999. We're seem to be now going further and deeper into 1999. The indictment finishes in September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The relevance relates to a series of questions and answers that were given by Mr. Stijovic in connection with the RDB's knowledge of the operation of paramilitary groupings on the territory of Kosovo and how that is to be reconciled with the evidence of this witness about RDB involvement with paramilitary groupings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in certain limits we'll allow you to these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll deal with it relatively briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did -- can you help us. As far as you understood the position, and based on the meeting you had on the 17th of May, did General Colonel Djordjevic have any responsibility for reintroducing the Skorpions into Kosovo after that incident?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why they were brought back after having been involved in a crime of that gravity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the information that General Colonel Djordjevic had been involved in that, that was information provided by Mr. Markovic, the head of the RDB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And is it also true that at that meeting Mr. Markovic -- I'm sorry, at that meeting with Mr. Markovic and Mr. Milosevic, the question of the deployment of Arkan's paramilitaries was raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I renew the objection. We're getting way beyond any, in my respectful submission, any latitude in relation to this questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Deep in 1999, in relation to Arkan. It's nine months after the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: With the greatest of respect, Mr. Re began his examination-in-chief by reference to a document exhibited by this witness concerning the deployment of Arkan's paramilitaries in January 1998 as to which this witness has testified, the connection between that deployment and the RDB, and that is what I'm seeking to explore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within certain limits you may proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, was it your understanding that Radomir Markovic had been involved in the deployment of Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that he was involved in that. I -- I should say that he gave his consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And returning, then, to the document that you exhibited to your witness statement and were taken to by Mr. Re. We have heard some testimony in this court from a man called Zoran Stijovic, who was head of the analytical section of the RDB in Pristina and who appeared to know you. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In your opinion as a military intelligence analyst, is it possible that Mr. Stijovic could have been ignorant of the deployment of paramilitary forces in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a hypothetical question, and I really can't give you an answer. I don't know if he was aware of that. I know what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Which is the involvement of the RDB directly with Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I've just told you. I believe that I gave you the gist of it so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, you -- you did give us the gist of it, but it may be that I've misunderstood your testimony. I thought the testimony that you gave us about the deployment in January of 1998 of Arkan's men was that that was a deployment organised by the State Security Service, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security sector was behind that. They knew of it. That's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I think it is in dispute, in fact, as between yourself and Mr. Stijovic. But -- but what I'm trying to understand is as an individual based in -- involved in counter-intelligence at the time and bearing in mind that Mr. Stijovic was head of the analytical section of the RDB in Pristina, whether in your opinion it is conceivable that he could not have known of that deployment.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that he didn't know. He was the head of analysis, and that department was able to work only on the basis of the reports it received. If there were no reports speaking of the presence of Arkan's unit there, he did not need to know about it, because he was not an operational officer; he was an analysis officer who analysed whatever came and ended up on his desk. If he didn't receive a report about the activities of a given unit, then he wouldn't know about it. Had he been an operations officer, the matter would stand differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you generally exchanging intelligence as between the RDB and your own counter-intelligence units?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were exchanging intelligence, but -- well, we let them know what our information was and, well, most often we didn't receive a response from them on that score. But we did exchange information wherever we thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there were matters of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you inform them from January 1998 that you were aware that paramilitaries were operating in the territory of Kosovo? Is that information that you provided to them as an exchange of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this exactly. It's been a long time ago. It's possible that we had our oral exchange of information so the head of the military intelligence could have informed the head of the RDB, Mr. Stanisic, I believe. At any rate, we never withheld from them any important information. We did not keep the information to ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Two final matters on this general topic, if I may. Colonel Crosland has testified to the Trial Chamber that during 1998 he observed groups of men he described as having the appearance of paramilitaries in the Decan area and followed them across the border into Montenegro, where they appeared to be rallying or corralling together. Can you help us at all as to the operation of paramilitary formations in the Western Kosovo area generally and in Decani in particular? In 1998.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in that period in the Decani area there was a group from the special police units, as far -- for a while there, but I -- I don't recall anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. And -- and the final question on this topic, and perhaps you can just deal with this very briefly: You testified in the Milutinovic trial about the infiltration into the 125th Brigade of a group called the Pauk Group or the Spider Group, led by Jugoslav Petrovic, who was believed to be an agent of French intelligence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't the case of an infiltration, as you put it; it was a volunteer unit of 23 men at the head of which was Jugoslav Petrusic, not Petrovic. Otherwise, a member of the French intelligence service and an agent of that service, which is something he confirmed to us when we spoke to him back in the month of May 1999. There is nothing controversial about that. He, I believe, was even the target of an investigation, but no evidence was found against him. But this was a volunteer unit that had passed the procedure in place and become formerly a volunteer unit. There is even an order of the commander of the 3rd Army to the effect that this unit should become part of the 125th Brigade. I repeat that the army did not have any paramilitary formations within its composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. Gajic, but when you testified in the Milutinovic trial you gave evidence that this group had sidestepped the regular procedure, that they had not gone through the appropriate vetting procedure, and that their entry into the ranks of the 125th had been organised by insiders acting improperly. Did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I spoke in no uncertain terms, and I even had a discussion with Judge Bonomy about that, because he didn't understand me. They were cleared -- I mean, they got the clearance after the vetting procedure, but the procedure was not thoroughly carried out. Had it been thoroughly done, half of them would not have passed it, because they had crime -- criminal records; they had been involved in robberies, and so on and so forth, and nevertheless got the clearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber now receives evidence about a 23-strong -- a 23-man-strong group led by someone who is supposed to be an agent for the French intelligence service. We have got no idea what we are talking about at this moment. So what the activities of this group were, whether you'd give that any follow-up, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about the formalities, rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I -- I take Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you help us very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any relevance in it. Of course, I do not know but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you help us, very briefly. When was that group in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the second half of April through to the first half of May. When we discovered that Jugoslav Petrusic was suspected of being a French agent, an agent of the French intelligence, the group was sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And this was -- sorry, this was 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want, if I may, to turn to the end of July operations that you have mentioned from time to time. Could you have a look, please, first of all, behind tab 16 in the bundle. And this is -- just bear with me one moment. This is a document not yet exhibited or marked for identification. And its identification number is 1D67-0001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked for identification as D187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, first of all, this is a document signed, as you can see, I think, by Colonel Delic on the 8th of August, 1998 which refers, as we can see in the opening words, to a strictly confidential order dated the 7th of August and sends an analysis of combat operations from the 18th of July to the 6th of August, 1998 along the axes in which the 549th Motorised Brigade took part. Now, my first question, before we look at the detail, Mr. -- Mr. Gajic, is: We have seen an entry in the minutes of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija for the 7th of August in which the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Sainovic, complains about the unnecessary destruction of civilian property during the course of this operation. Were you aware that such complaints were being expressed on a political level about the operation that had occurred at the end of July and the beginning of August?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know what this report is referring back to when it speaks of a strictly confidential order of the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report made by the command of 549th Brigade, signed by its commander, pursuant to the order of the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the date. Can Mr. Emmerson switch off his mic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It speaks of the analysis of the combat activities for the period between the 18th July and the 6th of August. Now, what was going on and what tasks were carried out in the area of the 549th Brigade. Well, I saw this report. I believe that under items 3 -- item 3 it speaks of the treatment of the civilian population, and so on and so forth. In any event, it's the sort of report that was normally done as a periodical analysis of the activities heretofore.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And all the units of the Pristina Corps submitted their respective reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned paragraph 3. And in the third subparagraph of that paragraph, the entry reads: "After the liberation of the place, there were incidents of theft and unnecessary destruction of property by MUP forces holding positions who were securing the liberated territory and by civilians from these areas out of revenge." Now, just to take this as one example that you say you saw at the time, Mr. Gajic, I'm trying to understand the testimony you gave us earlier when you said you never saw VJ reports of crimes committed by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This wasn't contained in any of the combat reports. This is the 549th Brigade report sent to the Pristina Corps from where reports were made and sent to the 3rd Army and then the 3rd Army in their turn sent reports to the Supreme Command. Why this wasn't entered into that particular report, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think we misunderstand each other. I think we misunderstand each other, Mr. Gajic. You told us a moment ago you saw this report at the time, and it makes reference to crimes committed by MUP forces. Now, a little earlier in your testimony, when I showed you the letter at tab 15 of the bundle from Colonel General Pavkovic, you said that you never saw a report during 1998 or 1999 of crimes committed by the MUP. Now, help us. What is the position? Did you or didn't you see reports from the VJ of crimes committed by the MUP? Any report.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we seem to be at cross-purposes at times, the two of us. I saw this report during proofing for my testimony here. It was at that point in time that this was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Gajic, that's not correct, I don't think, because it's not one of the exhibits to your statement. It's not one of the documents that you've been commenting upon. And it's not one of the documents that the Prosecution, so far as we're aware, have shown to you before. Now, the evidence you gave us a moment ago is that you'd seen the document at the time, as I understood it. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw this document during my proofing for this testimony. This is an original document of the 549th Brigade. The command reports of units did not reach the General Staff. Combat reports were sent to the General Staff, which presented --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think you should pause for a moment. I think you should pause for a moment. Mr. Re is sitting opposite me in the courtroom. This is a document that was not disclosed to the JDB and not a document provided by the Prosecution to us. If Mr. Re is in a position to confirm that he showed you this document in proofing, then now is the time for him to do it. I see no response. You're confident, are you, that this document was shown to you by proofing, in proofing sessions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. While I was being proofed here now, upon my arrival here, I was shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Well, if there's been a failure of communication between Prosecution and Defence, then that's not your responsibility. This is the first time, is it, you've seen a VJ report reporting crimes from the MUP? When you came here to -- to do the proofing for your statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document dated the 25th of May focused on item 4, war crimes committed against the civilian population. There was mention of murder, and so on and so forth. That's where the focus was and less focus was given to thefts, robberies, and so on and so forth. So it was the grave crimes that were being focused on. And as for these other matters, we did not -- and we did not receive any information on these crimes of any gravity in any of the combat reports; whereas, when it came to reports about theft, property crimes, well, we did see that. I mean, there was a war on and everybody is -- was engaged in that sort of misconduct. And the point was that once such crimes were reported on, they were supposed to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You put to the witness that he testified that he saw the document at the time. I have not found yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It may -- I mean, obviously I'm on my feet. It may be that I understood the answer in that way and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- the transcript does not reflect it. I'll obviously have to check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, just returning to this document, please, for a moment. Under paragraph 1, third bullet point, you can see the record that units of the 549th together with the 9th MUP Detachment were between the 2nd and 4th of August engaged in what is described as the liberation of the Mece village, Crmljane village, Crmljanska Kosa, Kraljane village axis. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to take up time producing a map, but can you please confirm for us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, where does it read that exactly? I see that under 1 it says that MUP forces were engaged on the same axis as combat groups of the -- Combat Group 1 of the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then later it says: "The MUP unit from Nis 9th was engaged in liberation" -- no, let me just -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under the -- well, let's say the fourth bullet point under there it says that: "The MUP unit, the 9th MUP Detachment, was engaged in" --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- I'm sorry, I'm reading the fourth bullet point in conjunction with the preamble in paragraph 1. Perhaps I should read the exact text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you are suggesting in your question -- you say you can see the record that units of the 549th together with. That's -- I -- that's more or less a conclusion interpretation. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it should be clear from --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What the preamble and paragraph -- the preamble indicates that it is an analysis of combat operations from the 18th of July to the 6th of August along the axes that the 549th Motorised Brigade took part. Paragraph 1 says: "Between the 18th of July and the 6th of August MUP forces were engaged on all the same axes as BG-1 of the 549th Motorised Brigade." And then as a subparagraph of that, bullet point 3 indicates that between the 2nd and the 4th of August, the MUP unit from Nis, the 9th MUP Detachment was engaged in the liberation of Mece village, Crmljane village, Crmljanska Kosa to Kraljane village axis." Now, I'm -- that -- that is the ipsissima verba of the text. My understanding of that is that was a joint -- as it indicates in paragraph 1, deployment of BG-1 of the 549th Motorised Brigade along that axis and the 9th MUP Detachment. I mean, if I'm -- if I appear to Your Honour to be misreading it, then obviously I'll stand corrected but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It reads the first they were engaged along the same axis. What is still to be established, whether this was a joint, coordinated action or whether it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, the one is a location.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That was not -- the reason for my error was that wasn't the focus specifically of the information I was seeking. But I take Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You would agree, would you, first of all, Mr. Gajic, that what this indicates by way of a report is that the BG-1 of the 549th was deployed along the same axis as the 9th MUP Detachment as appears in the bullet point 1.3?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were conducting a coordinated action. And under 1 bullet it says: The engaged MUP units were -- under 3, 9th Detachment; a group from Nis, had the strength of some 250 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Supported by -- and that means the 549th -- the 82-millimetre mortar detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So they were launching the activity; whereas, they had the support of the -- of a unit from the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think if we look a little further down in the document, two -- two paragraphs further down, there's a paragraph that indicates that the combat group in this composition provided support to the MUP forces and enabled them to carry out successful combat operations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You'll find that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What part are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you have it? I'm reading -- if you look at bullet point 1 -- the third bullet point 1 --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Page 1.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Page 1 in the B/C/S version, the paragraph just below halfway down. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. "The combat group in this composition provided support to the MUP forces and enabled it to carry out successful combat operations." Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Thank you. Now, Mece is a village along the main Gjakova-to-Klina road; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the next village from Mece is Crmljane and then Rakovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was unblocking the roads, to be precise. So that was the action to unblock the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. To your knowledge, were crimes committed during the course of that operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, during the course of the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, the Prosecution called a witness under the pseudonym K32, who testified that he had been conscripted in March 1998 and that in June 1998 he was assigned to the logistics corps in Prizren as a driver and then assigned to Combat Group 2 of the 549th under the command of General Delic. And amongst other matters, he testified that between the 1st and 3rd of August he was present with the VJ contingent on the operation on the main Gjakova-Klina road, including the village of Mece. He -- he testified that en route towards Mece, he came across a group of soldiers standing a few metres from the body of two Albanians who had been shot in the head and mutilated and was told by the soldiers that they had been captured, questioned, and then summarily killed. And on entry into Mece itself, he heard and saw Colonel Delic personally order a tank to open fire at a house, and after two shells had been fired, a group of civilians, mainly women and children, ran out of the house and Colonel Delic then sent in the infantry. Next he said the group entered Rakovina, where he saw MUP and PJP officers burning houses and looting property. And the references for those extracts are 8225 to 8228, 8320. No allegations of that crime found their way to you, so far as the VJ were concerned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And as far as I can remember, I listened to General Delic's testimony and I think he refuted that with strong arguments, even this witness's testimony and the statement of this witness that you mentioned. I don't know if you had an opportunity to study General Delic's evidence, and I think that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, just for the record, in order to avoid other people seeking for ages, your last reference was to 8230, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It should have been 8320. I don't know if it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it says 8320.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking is because our transcript behind tab 17 --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- goes until 8290.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I won't find it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It must in those circumstances, be my error in my notes and be 8230. If Your Honour would just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look at ... The events in Rakovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- are described in the lower part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 8230. So for the record, therefore, where you may have said and it was recorded 8320 should be 8230.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I ask you a little more, please, about the 52nd Military Police Battalion. In particular, in terms of the deployment that you describe in paragraph 22 of your witness statement, do you know who Major Janos Celj was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you didn't follow the testimony, obviously, then that he gave in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't listen to all the testimonies in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. And Major Celj was company commander of a unit called the 2nd Motorised Company, as we understand it. Can you help us as to where they were deployed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of which unit? It was the 2nd Company, but in which unit? In which brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, the record indicates -- the record indicates the 2nd Motorised Company of the -- I'll check to make absolutely certain I've got this correct -- of the 549th. Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Celj testified in the Milosevic trial that an individual by the name of Rade Radojevic -- that is Lieutenant Rade Radojevic was a commander commanding a battalion of the military police in August in the area securing the dam on the reservoir at Lake Radoniq. This is in the Milosevic transcript at page 47278. Does the name Rade Radojevic ring any bells to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Behind tab 18 is a conviction record - I'll see if it, perhaps, prompts your recollection at all - of a series of officers from within the -- or two officers from within the 549th, a conviction in September 2002 at the military court in Nis of Lieutenant Colonel Zlatan Mancic together with Rade Radojevic for the murder of two Albanian civilians in April 1999. And according to the record, Lieutenant Colonel Mancic was a senior officer within Combat Group 3 and Radojevic was his subordinate. Do you recall anything about this conviction?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, generally speaking, I can give you the following answer: Between the 1st and the 7th of June, 1999, I was with General Vasiljevic in Kosovo, and the subject matter there was, among other things, war crimes. As far as I can remember, there were 95 detected cases in which there were reasonable ground to suspect that war crimes were suspected. They were in a certain stage of procedure. Most probably these gentlemen were part of the procedure. If you are going to ask me about individual details, it is very difficult for me to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm -- what I'm interested in is that it appears that Mr. Radojevic, one of those, in fact, in the end convicted of murder of Albanian civilians, was in command of a military police battalion in the area of Lake Radoniq in August 1998. That's why I'm interested.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I am not contravening you. But what I said in principle is what I said before. All those who were detected at the time were within the certain procedures instituted against them. No one was forgiven for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. And you have no specific recollection of any connection between war crimes, prosecutions, and those in charge at -- of the Military Police Battalion or commanders located in the Lake Radoniq area in August 1998.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specifically I don't remember; however, it was found out that they had committed war crimes. Criminal reports were filed and proceedings instituted. And you said that punishments were pronounced. For instance, Lieutenant Colonel Stosic from the 37th Brigade and a group of soldier were also prosecuted and punished. Another officer with the 137 volunteers were -- was convicted to several years in prison. So all these procedures and proceedings were completed. As I said, no one has been forgiven for what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't remember this specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The question. I'm not interested in other instances but simply in the commanders stationed at the lake during the period that we're concerned with. If you have no recollection of that, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very close to concluding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. We would like to have a break, but we first ask the witness to leave the courtroom. We'll have a break. And then I'll further inquire into timing. And I might deliver ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not more than 15 minutes. Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll be extremely short. I believe I have one area, maybe two. I shouldn't be more than ten minutes. Maybe. Maybe -- maybe -- well, to be safe, say maybe 15. But that would be the absolute maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Makes 30. Yes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no plans for any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would take us half an hour. Mr. Re, how much time at this moment your estimate would be you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long does that leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Counting down from quarter to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather ask you how much time you would need and then see whether any time remains, because there are other matters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I would think between five and ten minutes. Not very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five to ten minutes. That leaves time now to read two decisions. The first decision is a decision on an application for videolink testimony. This is a decision on the Prosecution's application which was filed on the 19th of October, 2007 to have a witness's testimony heard by way of videolink connection with a location in the former Yugoslavia. I shall not name the witness in case an application for protective measures arises in the future. The witness is said to have serious health problems, making travel to The Hague unduly burdensome for him. The Prosecution asks for the witness's testimony to be heard on or about the 31st of October, 2007. This is relatively short notice, but the Registry apparently is able to meet the request if a decision is issued today. It is for this reason that the Chamber asked -- asked the Defence yesterday for an oral response, and the Defence kindly enough provided its response on the same day, informing us that it did not oppose the application. The witness in question has been issued with a subpoena, and therefore the question of his significance as a witness has already been determined. There remains the question of his health. The Chamber has seen a recent medical report on the witness which states that he suffers from high blood pressure as well as from spinal cord complaints causing dizziness and headache. All the medical records of the witness indicate a history of such complaints. In light of the information we have received, the Chamber believes that the witness's testimony through videolink is justified in his -- in this instance. We therefore request the Registrar to make the necessary arrangements. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's application. I will now deliver a decision on the admission of exhibits which were introduced through the Witness Crosland. On the 24th of May, 2007, the Chamber provisionally admitted, under seal, a number of documents which were exhibited in the Limaj case and which were tendered by the Prosecution in this case through witness Crosland. The relevant documents accompanied Mr. Crosland's testimony in the Limaj case, which has already been admitted in this case on the 19th of April, 2007 as Exhibit P69. There are 41 accompanying documents in total. The provisional nature of the admission of these documents was that, despite no objections from the Defence as to their admission, the Chamber wanted to study the documents which it had received only shortly before Mr. Crosland's testimony in order to be able to reach a final decision on their admission. After its review, the Chamber would then inform the parties whether any of the documents would be inadmissible. For reference on this, see transcript pages 4750 through 4753. Upon review, the Chamber found that five of these 41 exhibits had already been tendered by the Defence and admitted into evidence. These are Exhibits 76, 78, 81, 84, and 87; of course, all D numbers. These are respectively tabs 38, 39, 43, 46, and 34 in the Limaj exhibit binder provided to the Chamber and the Defence by the Prosecution. Furthermore, the document behind tab 15 of that binder, which was not MFI'd, was also tendered by the Defence and marked for identification as D110. This leaves us with 36 MFI'd documents from the Limaj case: D110 tendered by both the Defence and the Prosecution, and 35 documents tendered by the Prosecution as MFIs P819 through P853. However, out of these documents, MFI P822 is identical to MFI D107 and MFI P824 is identical to MFI D108. Since they are duplicates, we decide to strike MFIs D107 and D108 from the record. In relation to the old Rule 92 bis (D), which doesn't exist any more, at least not as it was, the Trial Chamber in the Naletilic and Martinovic case held that "Exhibits accompanying transcripts form an inseparable and indispensable part of the testimony and can be admitted along with the transcripts." This was a quote. This is in paragraph 8 of the "Decision Regarding Prosecutor's Notice of Intent to Offer Transcripts under Rule 92 bis (D)," which was filed on the 9th of July, 2001. We agree with this conclusion and consider that the 36 documents at issue here are so intrinsically linked to the transcript of Mr. Crosland's testimony in the Limaj case that they make up one inseparable body of evidence. As such, they should continue to be part of the record of the present case and are therefore admitted, under seal, without any further provision. Having decided that, the Chamber recalls that the Prosecution informed it that, in relation to the exhibits from the Limaj case, the British government provided the so-called dip-tels to the Prosecution under Rule 70. This is at page 2924. However, it may be that not all of the exhibits originating from the Limaj case were provided to the Prosecution under Rule 70, as some of them are not dip-tels and are documents which are originally in B/C/S. These are Exhibits P833, P838, P840, P841, P842, P844, and P848. We therefore invite the Prosecution to inform us, within a week from today, whether these seven exhibits can be unsealed. Finally, the Chamber further recalls that the Defence tendered six further documents through Mr. Crosland, which were MFI'd but not admitted. Two of these are photographs, MFIs D111 and D112; two are maps, D36 and D106; and two are Serbian military documents, MFIs D88 and D109. On the 25th of September, 2007, the Chamber's legal staff was informed by the Prosecution that it has no objection to the admission of these documents. In relation to D88, the Chamber notes that it's almost identical to Exhibit D34. The Chamber was informed by Mr. Emmerson on the 24th of May of 2007 in court that the parties had agreed that the two documents should be assigned different numbers and that the parties would ensure that the translations of the two documents are linked. This is at transcript pages 4752 and 4753. The two Serbian military documents tend to show the activities of the Serbian military forces in late May 1998 and the two photographs show a Serbian unit on a hill, albeit at an unknown date. D36 is a map marked by Mr. Crosland in court and D106 is a Serbian military map from 1998 depicting the area relevant to this case. The Chamber considers these documents relevant, as they tend to provide information on how the events related to the indictment unfolded; in particular, in relation to the armed conflict. We therefore admit these six documents, with a request to the registrar to note in the e-court system that Exhibits D34 and D88 are almost identical. And this concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. We will have a break until 1.00. Then the Chamber wants to stick very strictly to the time estimates, because it might leave some time, although limited, for other matters as well. We'll resume at 1.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I announced that we would be strict, we start.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, the last tab I want to ask you about is -- if you could please turn behind tab 19. And I'm going to ask some questions about Exhibit D146. And just so that we can orientate ourselves in this document, Mr. Gajic, this is an investigator's note of an interview with a man called Ersad Colovic, who was -- or is recorded as having been conscripted on the 18th of March, 1998 and assigned on the 8th of June, 1998 to the 549th Brigade, 2nd Motorised Company, 1st Motorised Platoon, 3rd Squad, stationed in Gjakova, and under the command of 2nd Lieutenant Rade Radojevic as his platoon commander. That's the gentleman who was the subject of the conviction we looked at behind the previous tab. And Major Janos Celj, as his company commander. The gentleman who's testimony I read to you from the Milosevic case a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think -- if we can turn, please, to page 5, which sets out those particulars and then -- just to confirm those. And then to page 11, where the substance of the report is set out. This individual reported to the Office of the Prosecutor that as part of the squad under the command of Lieutenant Rade Radojevic he was deployed in the area around Radoniq Lake until late August and took part in attacks on a number of villages in the area. And in particular, an attack is described in August of 1998 on the village of what is described as Gornji Brits, but I think is clearly given the geography, Gornji Bites, in these terms: "Most of the people" -- I'm looking at about halfway down the page. "Most of people who were killed were killed in their yards while they were trying to flee. We used to use anti-tank anti-armour launchers into houses. This killed a lot of people. Orders were to kill people in their yards or in front of their houses. Not everyone was killed. One group we would get orders to kill everyone, so we would kill everyone. With other groups, we would be under orders not to kill, so we would let them all go. The major made these orders and the second lieutenant sometimes, mostly the major. The largest group of persons killed that I am aware was ten persons (women and children). This happens in G. Brits, Gornji Brits. It was in August. We entered the village. We were under orders. We found the group and we were under orders to kill them, so we did." And a little further down he describes the people as women in their 30s and 40s, men in their 50s, two children, about 12 or 13 years old. And he says: "No one lived. They all died. They were all executed. They were shot at by two squads who received orders to kill them. One of those squads was my squad." And he a little later on he says that he and the soldiers with him stayed in the area that night, but by the morning the bodies were gone." And at the bottom of the page: "The dead bodies would not be there the next morning. They were collected by the militia." Were you aware of VJ involvement during August in military activities in Gornji Bites?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I said that I wasn't aware of this incident when you asked me about it. If this is indeed how things transpired, there was criminal prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in -- against the people involved, against the commanding officers. As for this specific case, I'm not aware of it at all. This is a statement of one witness. I don't know if there are other statements corroborating this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any misunderstanding, this is not the same incident as the incident for which Mr. Radojevic was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Emmerson, you asked whether the witness was aware of VJ involvement during August in military activities in this place. There's no need for you to say this is just one statement. It's -- of course, the Chamber -- if it's only one statement, the Chamber is aware of it; if there are more statements, you might not know about it. That's -- but your answer was clear. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you have any reports of operations in Gornji Bites or those villages during August, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally didn't receive any such reports, and this is the first time I hear of it, of the things you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Gajic, you'll now be further cross-examined by Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Guy-Smith does that, tab 17, the transcript of the testimony of Witness K32 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- is not yet marked for identification. It's Defence Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, could you assign a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be marked for identification as D188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And tab 18 is the conviction document for Mr. Radojevic, which is Defence 1D67-0087.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked for identification as D189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could I invite the parties to see what is needed to get an idea of the context and what is not needed to have an idea about the context, because both 17 and 18 are rather lengthy documents. So perhaps the size could be reduced, taking out matters that are less relevant. But that could even be done at a later stage. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith is Defence counsel for Mr. Balaj, and he'll now further cross-examine you, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony earlier that sometime around the 29th of July there was what I understood - and I'm hoping you can help me - an operation that you called Grom-3. And my question to you is: Was there an operation in 1998 which was known by the name of Grom, or Grom, which I understand means "Thunder," which was an operation involving the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was an operation in which the VJ was involved pursuant to the directive issued by the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the operation called the Grom Operation, which -- which we're talking about, that's an operation that began in July; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same operation. It's just that its code name was Grom-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before July, I take it there was no implementation of the Operation Grom within the VJ. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Up to that point it was the MUP that launched all the activities against the terrorists with -- acting in coordination with the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you say it was the MUP who was launching all the activities against the terrorists in coordination with the VJ, were they operating under that same plan? Was that also the Grom Operation? Or was that a different -- did that operation have a different name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't the operation. There existed a plan of combat against the terrorist forces, but it did not have a title such as Operation Grom, but nothing that was done outside of a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So just so I'm very clear, before July any operation that existed was an operation that was launched by MUP. It did not have a name, and it was in coordination with the VJ. And after July, then there was Operation Grom. Am I correct in -- in my understanding?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct in your understanding. I repeat, before the month of July there existed a plan. There is always a plan in place when you're deploying forces, especially when you're deploying combined forces, such as the VJ and the MUP. Now, Operation Grom-3 was a separate operation that was carried out in the months of July, August, and ended in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But before that time, there -- there was no -- there was no operation involving MUP that was called Operation Grom, was there? That was specifically defined --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apologies. It wasn't called that way, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked a question earlier about whether or not there were any special police units in the Decani area in 1998, and I believe your response was that you believed that there were some but that you couldn't recall anything further. I'm wondering whether or not you -- have you ever heard of a police unit called the Munja Group that operated in this area in 1998.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not aware of a unit with such a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about an individual by the name of Nebojsa Minic, who I believe his nickname was Mrtiv or "death", who operated in this area during 1998? And by "this area," I'm talking about, obviously, Decani area.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about an individual by the name of Vidomir Salipur who was a member of any police unit or special unit operating during that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I never heard about such an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. One -- and one last -- one last name, which is Srdan - and I could be pronouncing it incorrectly, and if I am, I apologise. That's S-r-d-a-n, last name is Perovic, who I believe was a deputy company commander. And that would have probably been in some part of the MUP, but I'm not exactly sure exactly which part. Does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name of Srdjan Perovic. He was a captain. If that's the same person. Srdjan Perovic was a captain of the police who had been captured by the KLA. He was killed later on, and we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the findings, the pathological findings, and so on and so forth. If that's the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to see if you can help us with regard to a particular document in -- in light of -- of some of the answers given. And perhaps you can clear something up for us, if you could, and we can see D162, marked for identification. And I'm hoping that you can help us just with -- with one part. As I understand the document, the date is the 24th of June, 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would be sometime before the month of July, if I'm not mistaken, about a month before July 29th. Right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The subject of the document is report on the measures and actions taken to protect damaged and abandoned property and on the legality of police actions during Operation Grom, "Thunder," for the period from 29 May 1998 to 20 June 1998. As I understand this document - and this is where I'd like some help for you, especially in light of the answers you've just given - this document reflects that the police were involved in Operation Grom beginning at the end of May through close to the end of June approximately a month before you have told us that the operation itself started with the VJ. Could you -- could you be of some help with that, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- if I can be of assistance. The name Grom denoted the general plan for Kosovo and Metohija in relation to the resolution of the problems there. Most probably the colleagues from the MUP were aware of this name and used it in order to have some sort of a cover of -- for what was done. As far as the army is concerned and the execution of operations, until Operation Grom-3 there had been no named operations that were carried out. I suppose the colleagues in the MUP knew of this name and then christened this activity this way, so to speak. It -- anyway, what is stated here has to do with the activities carried out by the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. It has nothing to do with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So any activity that -- as far as I can tell from this document, any activity under the auspices of -- of the name "Operation Grom" from the period of the 29th of May through June was an operation that was solely a MUP operation and had absolutely nothing to do with -- with the VJ. Is -- is that your evidence? Just so I'm clear.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Yugoslav Army was acting in coordination with the MUP in this period too. Now, the MUP probably named all their operations as part of that operation, Operation Grom. They did all that under that cover of -- of the operation; whereas, the Yugoslav Army provided support. They acted in coordination with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've used the word "probably" on -- on a number of occasions and in response to -- to why this document is entitled "Operation Grom." I take it that you have never received any specific information yourself in the position that you had that MUP was operating under Operation Grom during this period of time or any other period of time before July 29th, 1998. Is that correct? You have no documentation or ever saw any documentation that indicated this. This is the first time you've seen anything that indicates that MUP was operating under the -- the Grom plan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under that name, yes. We received reports through the line of command. And as I said, the VJ acted in coordinated action with the MUP, but we did not receive a single document about it from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Still no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still no questions. Mr. Re, is there any need to re-examine the witness? Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. There are several matters. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, today Mr. Emmerson asked you some questions, mainly at page 31 of the transcript, in relation to Colonel Crosland and his view of the number of fighters or hard-core fighters there were in Kosovo in 1998, and you expressed a different opinion to his. Just to clarify further what you said, can you tell the Trial Chamber what information you had access to or would have had access to at that time which Colonel Crosland would not have had access to which enables you to form a different view.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information from the field, from many more sources than Mr. Crosland could have had. I said that I know him personally, and I hold him in high esteem, but still we had the information down -- reaching us down the line of command. Then we had information from special services, the military counter-intelligence service, the intelligence service of the MUP. Then we had information reaching us through electronic surveillance, information through the reconnaissance organs of the Army of Yugoslavia, and information coming from members of the KLA we had captured. There were quite a few such individuals who through investigations told us the head count of KLA members. Their weapons, how many of them were involved in these activities, how many of them were not, how many of them had weapons at home and had not. And then there were border units of the VJ that had captured many KLA members who were coming over from Albania, and through interviews with them we were able to know what was going on in Albania in the various villages there. These were all the diverse information we collated, cross-referenced, and arrived at pretty reliable information at the end of that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why do you say it's reliable? You said it's pretty reliable. Why?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because they came from several sources. Normally when you have information from a single source or from two sources, then that information is to be taken with much more reservations than information arriving from several sources. Though, I have to tell you that we always used approximate terminology. We never said -- or wrote anything in a resolute manner. We would always use the terms "approximately," "circa," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson also asked you about the assessment of 200 men being engaged as peaceful farmers by day and KLA soldiers by night. That was at page 37 and in relation to MFI P1142. And you were giving an answer to Mr. Emmerson in which you said: "That was the tactics that they used and they were successful in doing so." Based upon everything you saw, observed, heard, the reports you saw, what is your assessment of why they were so successful in adopting those tactics?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, let me tell you this: I spoke about the 200 men you referred to just now, and I said that those were 200 men who were organised in the various groups; whereas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Re, follow-up questions showed that these farmers by day, soldiers by night were above the 200, and this might also give some clue where Colonel Crosland gave estimates or whether he -- when he commented on it. He was talking about core KLA people. There seems to be a distinction between those who were really engaged in the core of the KLA and those who participated in their activities, although perhaps not full time. But this issue, the witness corrects you rightly, because in the follow-up questions this confusion has been set aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking about. I'm asking about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But you're introducing the question, and the witness starts commenting on that, that you are more or less misquoting, because your question started by saying - let me just stop the transcript - "Mr. Emmerson asked you about the assessment of 200 men being engaged as peaceful farmers by day and KLA soldiers by night." As a matter of fact, this was above the number, in addition to the number of, I take it, more-intensely-engaged KLA members. The answer was in the beginning a bit ambiguous, but it has been clarified through follow-up questions. And that's where the witness now is seeking to correct your -- the way in which you reflect his testimony, which was actually not correct. But let's -- please proceed, because you -- That is fully understood, Mr. Gajic. Now Mr. Re would like to know what you meant by that this was the tactics they used and were successful in doing so, what you meant by that. That's what the question focuses upon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I understand.
